claim: Several discrete groups of feeding-regulated neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) suppress food intake.
source: Several discrete groups of feeding-regulated neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius; NTS) suppress food intake, including avoidance-promoting neurons that express Cck (NTSCck cells) and distinct Lepr- and Calcr-expressing neurons (NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cells, respectively) that suppress food intake without promoting avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work and the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: NTSCck cells are avoidance-promoting neurons.
source: Several discrete groups of feeding-regulated neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius; NTS) suppress food intake, including avoidance-promoting neurons that express Cck (NTSCck cells) and distinct Lepr- and Calcr-expressing neurons (NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cells, respectively) that suppress food intake without promoting avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by characterization of NTSCck cells as avoidance-promoting in the abstract and throughout the manuscript.

claim: NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cells suppress food intake without promoting avoidance.
source: Several discrete groups of feeding-regulated neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius; NTS) suppress food intake, including avoidance-promoting neurons that express Cck (NTSCck cells) and distinct Lepr- and Calcr-expressing neurons (NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cells, respectively) that suppress food intake without promoting avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing these cells suppress feeding without causing conditioned taste avoidance.

claim: Activating multiple sets of NTS neurons (e.g. NTSLepr plus NTSCalcr [NTSLC], or NTSLC plus NTSCck [NTSLCK]) suppressed feeding more robustly than activating single populations.
source: We found that activating multiple sets of NTS neurons (e.g. NTSLepr plus NTSCalcr [NTSLC], or NTSLC plus NTSCck [NTSLCK]) suppressed feeding more robustly than activating single populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DREADD activation studies shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Activating groups of cells that include NTSCck neurons promoted conditioned taste avoidance (CTA).
source: While activating groups of cells that include NTSCck neurons promoted conditioned taste avoidance (CTA), NTSLC activation produced no CTA despite abrogating feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: NTSLC activation produced no CTA despite abrogating feeding.
source: While activating groups of cells that include NTSCck neurons promoted conditioned taste avoidance (CTA), NTSLC activation produced no CTA despite abrogating feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: The ability to promote CTA formation represents a dominant effect.
source: Thus, the ability to promote CTA formation represents a dominant effect but activating multiple non-aversive populations augments the suppression of food intake without provoking avoidance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that any combination including NTSCck cells promotes CTA.

claim: Activating multiple non-aversive populations augments the suppression of food intake without provoking avoidance.
source: Thus, the ability to promote CTA formation represents a dominant effect but activating multiple non-aversive populations augments the suppression of food intake without provoking avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing NTSLC activation suppresses feeding more than single populations without causing CTA.

claim: Silencing multiple NTS neuron groups augmented food intake and body weight to a greater extent than silencing single populations.
source: Furthermore, silencing multiple NTS neuron groups augmented food intake and body weight to a greater extent than silencing single populations, consistent with the notion that each of these NTS neuron populations plays crucial and cumulative roles in the control of energy balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by TetTox silencing experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Each of these NTS neuron populations plays crucial and cumulative roles in the control of energy balance.
source: Furthermore, silencing multiple NTS neuron groups augmented food intake and body weight to a greater extent than silencing single populations, consistent with the notion that each of these NTS neuron populations plays crucial and cumulative roles in the control of energy balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative effects observed when silencing multiple populations.

claim: Silencing NTSLCK neurons failed to blunt the weight-loss response to vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG).
source: We found that silencing NTSLCK neurons failed to blunt the weight-loss response to vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG) and that feeding activated many non-NTSLCK neurons, however, suggesting that as-yet undefined NTS cell types must make additional contributions to the restraint of feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Feeding activated many non-NTSLCK neurons.
source: We found that silencing NTSLCK neurons failed to blunt the weight-loss response to vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG) and that feeding activated many non-NTSLCK neurons, however, suggesting that as-yet undefined NTS cell types must make additional contributions to the restraint of feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: As-yet undefined NTS cell types must make additional contributions to the restraint of feeding.
source: We found that silencing NTSLCK neurons failed to blunt the weight-loss response to vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG) and that feeding activated many non-NTSLCK neurons, however, suggesting that as-yet undefined NTS cell types must make additional contributions to the restraint of feeding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that many non-NTSLCK neurons are activated by feeding and that silencing NTSLCK cells doesn't prevent VSG effects.

claim: The ongoing obesity pandemic represents an enormous challenge to human health and longevity.
source: The ongoing obesity pandemic represents an enormous challenge to human health and longevity (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to CDC data.

claim: Many hypothalamic circuits act via the brainstem to suppress food intake.
source: While hypothalamic circuits contribute to the control of feeding and play important roles in maintaining long-term energy balance, many hypothalamic circuits act via the brainstem to suppress food intake (Cheng et al., 2022; Grill, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brainstem receives feeding-related and other information from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
source: Furthermore, the brainstem receives feeding-related and other information from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, controls the rhythmic pattern generators that mediate feeding, and can overcome hypothalamically-driven hyperphagia (Cheng et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brainstem controls the rhythmic pattern generators that mediate feeding.
source: Furthermore, the brainstem receives feeding-related and other information from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, controls the rhythmic pattern generators that mediate feeding, and can overcome hypothalamically-driven hyperphagia (Cheng et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brainstem can overcome hypothalamically-driven hyperphagia.
source: Furthermore, the brainstem receives feeding-related and other information from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, controls the rhythmic pattern generators that mediate feeding, and can overcome hypothalamically-driven hyperphagia (Cheng et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many of the most important food intake-controlling brainstem systems lie in the dorsal vagal complex (DVC).
source: Many of the most important food intake-controlling brainstem systems lie in the dorsal vagal complex (DVC), which includes the area postrema (AP), the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV; Cheng et al., 2022; Grill, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dorsal vagal complex (DVC) includes the area postrema (AP), the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV).
source: Many of the most important food intake-controlling brainstem systems lie in the dorsal vagal complex (DVC), which includes the area postrema (AP), the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV; Cheng et al., 2022; Grill, 2014).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited in the manuscript.

claim: The AP lies outside of the blood-brain barrier.
source: The AP lies outside of the blood-brain barrier and receives circulating signals relevant to feeding, including from several anorexigenic peptides.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The AP receives circulating signals relevant to feeding, including from several anorexigenic peptides.
source: The AP lies outside of the blood-brain barrier and receives circulating signals relevant to feeding, including from several anorexigenic peptides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AP function.

claim: The NTS lies adjacent to and receives input from the AP.
source: The NTS, which lies adjacent to and receives input from the AP, also receives input from GI-innervating vagal sensory neurons.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The NTS receives input from GI-innervating vagal sensory neurons.
source: The NTS, which lies adjacent to and receives input from the AP, also receives input from GI-innervating vagal sensory neurons.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Both the AP and NTS project ventrally to the DMV to control GI motility and other physiological functions.
source: Both the AP and NTS project ventrally to the DMV to control GI motility and other physiological functions, in addition to innervating more rostral brain regions to modulate food intake.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge.

claim: The AP and NTS innervate more rostral brain regions to modulate food intake.
source: Both the AP and NTS project ventrally to the DMV to control GI motility and other physiological functions, in addition to innervating more rostral brain regions to modulate food intake.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge.

claim: Many brainstem circuits express receptors for peptides that suppress food intake, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R).
source: Many of these brainstem circuits express receptors for peptides that suppress food intake, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R); the calcitonin receptor (CALCR) and the related amylin receptor (AmyR- a complex of CALCR and a receptor activity modifying protein [RAMP]); and the leptin receptor (LepRb) (Cheng et al., 2022; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many brainstem circuits express the calcitonin receptor (CALCR) and the related amylin receptor (AmyR).
source: Many of these brainstem circuits express receptors for peptides that suppress food intake, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R); the calcitonin receptor (CALCR) and the related amylin receptor (AmyR- a complex of CALCR and a receptor activity modifying protein [RAMP]); and the leptin receptor (LepRb) (Cheng et al., 2022; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The amylin receptor (AmyR) is a complex of CALCR and a receptor activity modifying protein (RAMP).
source: Many of these brainstem circuits express receptors for peptides that suppress food intake, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R); the calcitonin receptor (CALCR) and the related amylin receptor (AmyR- a complex of CALCR and a receptor activity modifying protein [RAMP]); and the leptin receptor (LepRb) (Cheng et al., 2022; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about receptor structure.

claim: Many brainstem circuits express the leptin receptor (LepRb).
source: Many of these brainstem circuits express receptors for peptides that suppress food intake, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R); the calcitonin receptor (CALCR) and the related amylin receptor (AmyR- a complex of CALCR and a receptor activity modifying protein [RAMP]); and the leptin receptor (LepRb) (Cheng et al., 2022; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many DVC cell types may contribute to the suppression of feeding by gut peptide mimetics currently under development or in use for weight loss therapy.
source: Thus, many of these DVC cell types may contribute to the suppression of feeding by a variety of gut peptide mimetics currently under development or in use for weight loss therapy (Cheng et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression of relevant receptors in DVC cells.

claim: The AP and NTS neuron types that suppress food intake while mediating avoidance responses are distinct from neuron types that promote the non-aversive suppression of food intake.
source: Recent work from others and us has demonstrated that the AP and NTS neuron types that suppress food intake while mediating avoidance responses associated with gut malaise are distinct from neuron types that promote the non-aversive suppression of food intake (Cheng et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021; Roman et al., 2017; Palmiter, 2017; Campos et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cell types that suppress food intake without causing avoidance include NTS neurons that express Lepr (NTSLepr cells) or Calcr (NTSCalcr cells).
source: Cell types that suppress food intake without causing avoidance include NTS neurons that express Lepr (NTSLepr cells) or Calcr (NTSCalcr cells); in contrast, Cck-expressing NTS neurons (NTSCck cells) promote avoidance (Cheng et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cck-expressing NTS neurons (NTSCck cells) promote avoidance.
source: Cell types that suppress food intake without causing avoidance include NTS neurons that express Lepr (NTSLepr cells) or Calcr (NTSCalcr cells); in contrast, Cck-expressing NTS neurons (NTSCck cells) promote avoidance (Cheng et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Each of these cell types represent excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons.
source: Each of these cell types represent excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons Ludwig et al., 2021a; these neurons also contain the neuropeptides glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1; NTSLepr neurons), prolactin releasing peptide (PrRP; NTSCalcr neurons), and cholecystokinin (CCK; NTSCck neurons) (Cheng et al., 2021; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Huo et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NTSLepr neurons contain the neuropeptide glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1).
source: Each of these cell types represent excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons Ludwig et al., 2021a; these neurons also contain the neuropeptides glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1; NTSLepr neurons), prolactin releasing peptide (PrRP; NTSCalcr neurons), and cholecystokinin (CCK; NTSCck neurons) (Cheng et al., 2021; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Huo et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSCalcr neurons contain the neuropeptide prolactin releasing peptide (PrRP).
source: Each of these cell types represent excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons Ludwig et al., 2021a; these neurons also contain the neuropeptides glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1; NTSLepr neurons), prolactin releasing peptide (PrRP; NTSCalcr neurons), and cholecystokinin (CCK; NTSCck neurons) (Cheng et al., 2021; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Huo et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSCck neurons contain the neuropeptide cholecystokinin (CCK).
source: Each of these cell types represent excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons Ludwig et al., 2021a; these neurons also contain the neuropeptides glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1; NTSLepr neurons), prolactin releasing peptide (PrRP; NTSCalcr neurons), and cholecystokinin (CCK; NTSCck neurons) (Cheng et al., 2021; Ludwig et al., 2021a; Huo et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bariatric surgeries, including vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG), decrease meal size and overall food intake to promote dramatic weight loss in many patients.
source: Bariatric surgeries, including vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG), decrease meal size and overall food intake to promote dramatic weight loss in many patients (Peterli et al., 2018), as well as in animal models of VSG (Stefater et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical and animal studies.

claim: VSG decreases meal size and overall food intake in animal models.
source: Bariatric surgeries, including vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG), decrease meal size and overall food intake to promote dramatic weight loss in many patients (Peterli et al., 2018), as well as in animal models of VSG (Stefater et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: The irreversibility and side effects of VSG, together with the inability to perform enough surgeries to treat the number of patients in need, prevents the use of this intervention at a population scale.
source: The irreversibility and side effects of the procedure, together with the inability to perform enough surgeries to treat the number of patients in need, prevents the use of this intervention at a population scale, however (Altieri et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation discussing limitations of bariatric surgery.

claim: CNO treatment promoted FOS-immunoreactivity in the NTS of LeprDq, CalcrDq and LCDq mice.
source: As expected, CNO treatment promoted FOS-immunoreactivity (-IR) in the NTS of LeprDq, CalcrDq and LCDq mice, with the LCDq mice displaying increased FOS-IR compared to animals in which we had transduced only one population (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LCDq mice displayed increased FOS-IR compared to animals in which only one population was transduced.
source: As expected, CNO treatment promoted FOS-immunoreactivity (-IR) in the NTS of LeprDq, CalcrDq and LCDq mice, with the LCDq mice displaying increased FOS-IR compared to animals in which we had transduced only one population (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed LeprDq and CalcrDq mice.
source: As we showed previously (Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b), CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed LeprDq and CalcrDq mice; LCDq mice responded similarly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LCDq mice responded similarly to LeprDq and CalcrDq mice in terms of CNO-mediated suppression of food intake at the onset of the dark cycle.
source: As we showed previously (Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b), CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed LeprDq and CalcrDq mice; LCDq mice responded similarly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The activation of NTSLepr neurons tended to suppress feeding less than NTSCalcr and NTSLC neurons at the 4 hr time point in HFD-fed mice at the onset of the dark cycle.
source: The same was true for mice fed high-fat diet (HFD) at the onset at the dark cycle, although the activation of NTSLepr neurons tended to suppress feeding less than NTSCalcr and NTSLC neurons at the 4 hr time point in this assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Following an overnight fast, the activation of NTSLepr neurons significantly decreased refeeding over 6 hr.
source: Following an overnight fast, the activation of NTSLepr neurons significantly decreased refeeding over 6 hr; the activation of NTSCalcr cells alone decreased refeeding further than NTSLepr neurons, and the activation of NTSLC neurons decreased refeeding even further- by approximately 90% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The activation of NTSCalcr cells alone decreased refeeding further than NTSLepr neurons.
source: Following an overnight fast, the activation of NTSLepr neurons significantly decreased refeeding over 6 hr; the activation of NTSCalcr cells alone decreased refeeding further than NTSLepr neurons, and the activation of NTSLC neurons decreased refeeding even further- by approximately 90% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The activation of NTSLC neurons decreased refeeding by approximately 90%.
source: Following an overnight fast, the activation of NTSLepr neurons significantly decreased refeeding over 6 hr; the activation of NTSCalcr cells alone decreased refeeding further than NTSLepr neurons, and the activation of NTSLC neurons decreased refeeding even further- by approximately 90% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activating NTSLepr neurons decreased feeding and body weight over a two-day treatment.
source: Similarly, activating NTSLepr neurons decreased feeding and body weight over a two-day treatment, activating NTSCalcr neurons suppressed these parameters more effectively, and activating both cell types in LCDq mice reduced feeding by >90% for the first 24 hr and continued to reduce food intake compared to the individual cell types during the second 24 hr of the experiment (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic treatment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Activating NTSCalcr neurons suppressed feeding and body weight more effectively than activating NTSLepr neurons.
source: Similarly, activating NTSLepr neurons decreased feeding and body weight over a two-day treatment, activating NTSCalcr neurons suppressed these parameters more effectively, and activating both cell types in LCDq mice reduced feeding by >90% for the first 24 hr and continued to reduce food intake compared to the individual cell types during the second 24 hr of the experiment (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic treatment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Activating both NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cell types in LCDq mice reduced feeding by >90% for the first 24 hr.
source: Similarly, activating NTSLepr neurons decreased feeding and body weight over a two-day treatment, activating NTSCalcr neurons suppressed these parameters more effectively, and activating both cell types in LCDq mice reduced feeding by >90% for the first 24 hr and continued to reduce food intake compared to the individual cell types during the second 24 hr of the experiment (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic treatment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: CNO treatment was discontinued after 48 hr because of animal welfare concerns due to the amount of weight loss exhibited by the LCDq mice.
source: While we had intended to continue treatment for another day, we discontinued CNO treatment after 48 hr because of animal welfare concerns due to the amount of weight loss exhibited by the LCDq mice.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental procedures and observations.

claim: NTSCalcr neurons suppress feeding more robustly than NTSLepr neurons.
source: Hence, NTSCalcr neurons suppress feeding more robustly than NTSLepr neurons, and NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons suppress feeding cumulatively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative feeding suppression data.

claim: NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons suppress feeding cumulatively.
source: Hence, NTSCalcr neurons suppress feeding more robustly than NTSLepr neurons, and NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons suppress feeding cumulatively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that activating both populations suppresses feeding more than either alone.

claim: The gut malaise associated with LiCl injection promoted a robust CTA to the novel exposure to HFD.
source: We found that, although the gut malaise associated with LiCl injection promoted a robust CTA to either the novel exposure to HFD or saccharine in drinking water, NTSLC activation failed to provoke such a response (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The gut malaise associated with LiCl injection promoted a robust CTA to saccharine in drinking water.
source: We found that, although the gut malaise associated with LiCl injection promoted a robust CTA to either the novel exposure to HFD or saccharine in drinking water, NTSLC activation failed to provoke such a response (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: NTSLC activation failed to provoke a CTA to HFD or saccharine.
source: We found that, although the gut malaise associated with LiCl injection promoted a robust CTA to either the novel exposure to HFD or saccharine in drinking water, NTSLC activation failed to provoke such a response (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The coordinated activation of two non-aversive cell types (NTSLepr and NTSCalcr) fails to promote a CTA despite almost abolishing food intake.
source: Thus, the coordinated activation of two non-aversive cell types (NTSLepr and NTSCalcr Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017) fails to promote a CTA despite almost abolishing food intake.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CTA and feeding data.

claim: CNO failed to significantly increase food intake during the first four hours of the dark cycle in LCDi mice expressing hM4Di in NTSLC cells.
source: While CNO failed to significantly increase food intake during the first four hours of the dark cycle, stimulating hM4Di in NTSLC cells increased food intake during refeeding with chow or HFD following an overnight fast.
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stimulating hM4Di in NTSLC cells increased food intake during refeeding with chow or HFD following an overnight fast.
source: While CNO failed to significantly increase food intake during the first four hours of the dark cycle, stimulating hM4Di in NTSLC cells increased food intake during refeeding with chow or HFD following an overnight fast.
evidence: This claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: NTSLC neurons contribute to the restraint of food intake during refeeding.
source: Thus, NTSLC neurons contribute to the restraint of food intake during refeeding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased refeeding observed when NTSLC neurons are inhibited.

claim: Long-term tetanus toxin (TetTox)-mediated silencing of NTSCalcr neurons promotes increased food intake and body weight in animals exposed to HFD.
source: We previously showed that the long-term tetanus toxin (TetTox)-mediated silencing of NTSCalcr neurons promotes increased food intake and body weight in animals exposed to HFD (Cheng et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LeprTetTox mice displayed no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding for LeprTetTox mice, these animals displayed a modest increase in food intake on HFD and gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: LeprTetTox mice displayed a modest increase in food intake on HFD.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding for LeprTetTox mice, these animals displayed a modest increase in food intake on HFD and gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LeprTetTox mice gained more body weight over 6 weeks on HFD than control animals.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding for LeprTetTox mice, these animals displayed a modest increase in food intake on HFD and gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NTSLepr neurons contribute to the long-term control of energy balance.
source: Thus, NTSLepr neurons (like NTSCalcr cells) contribute to the long-term control of energy balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased body weight observed in LeprTetTox mice on HFD.

claim: LCTetTox mice displayed no significant increase in food intake or body weight during 6 weeks of chow feeding compared to controls.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during 6 weeks of chow feeding in LCTetTox mice compared to controls, LCTetTox mice ate significantly more food and gained (~10 grams) more body weight than controls when exposed to HFD for 6 weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and H.

claim: LCTetTox mice ate significantly more food when exposed to HFD for 6 weeks.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during 6 weeks of chow feeding in LCTetTox mice compared to controls, LCTetTox mice ate significantly more food and gained (~10 grams) more body weight than controls when exposed to HFD for 6 weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: LCTetTox mice gained approximately 10 grams more body weight than controls when exposed to HFD for 6 weeks.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during 6 weeks of chow feeding in LCTetTox mice compared to controls, LCTetTox mice ate significantly more food and gained (~10 grams) more body weight than controls when exposed to HFD for 6 weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Continuous analysis of feeding demonstrated increased food intake by LCTetTox mice in the dark (active) cycle.
source: Continuous analysis of feeding demonstrated increased food intake by LCTetTox mice in the dark (active) cycle, consistent with decreased suppression of food intake in response to normal feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by continuous feeding data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased food intake by LCTetTox mice in the dark cycle is consistent with decreased suppression of food intake in response to normal feeding.
source: Continuous analysis of feeding demonstrated increased food intake by LCTetTox mice in the dark (active) cycle, consistent with decreased suppression of food intake in response to normal feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the feeding pattern data.

claim: Silencing multiple NTS neuron populations (as in LCTetTox mice) increases feeding and weight gain relative to silencing single populations.
source: While comparing results among different strains of mice studied at different times requires cautious interpretation, these findings suggest that the silencing of multiple NTS neuron populations (as in LCTetTox mice) increases feeding and weight gain relative to silencing single populations (NTSLepr in the current study, as well as previously-studied NTSCalcr cells previously Cheng et al., 2020a; Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of data across different TetTox mouse lines, shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HFD-fed LCTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of VSG surgery.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed LCTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG also promoted more weight loss in these animals than in controls (both in terms of total weight lost and percent body weight lost) and similarly improved measures of glycemic control.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VSG promoted more weight loss in LCTetTox mice than in controls (both in terms of total weight lost and percent body weight lost).
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed LCTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG also promoted more weight loss in these animals than in controls (both in terms of total weight lost and percent body weight lost) and similarly improved measures of glycemic control.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: VSG similarly improved measures of glycemic control in LCTetTox and control mice.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed LCTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG also promoted more weight loss in these animals than in controls (both in terms of total weight lost and percent body weight lost) and similarly improved measures of glycemic control.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J-L.

claim: NTSLC neurons are not required for VSG-mediated weight loss.
source: Thus, NTSLC neurons are not required for VSG-mediated weight loss, and other cell types must contribute to the suppression of food intake following VSG.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VSG still promotes weight loss in LCTetTox mice.

claim: Other cell types must contribute to the suppression of food intake following VSG.
source: Thus, NTSLC neurons are not required for VSG-mediated weight loss, and other cell types must contribute to the suppression of food intake following VSG.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VSG still promotes weight loss when NTSLC neurons are silenced.

claim: Activation of NTSCck neurons promotes avoidance (e.g. CTA) responses, as well as decreasing feeding.
source: While NTSLepr and NTSCalcr cells both mediate the non-aversive suppression of food intake, activation of NTSCck neurons promotes avoidance (e.g. CTA) responses, as well as decreasing feeding (Cheng et al., 2020a; Roman et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2020b; Roman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CckTetTox mice displayed no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding for CckTetTox mice, these animals gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals during HFD feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: CckTetTox mice gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals during HFD feeding.
source: While we detected no significant increase in food intake or body weight during chow feeding for CckTetTox mice, these animals gained more body weight over 6 weeks than control animals during HFD feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Silencing NTSCck neurons might impact body weight by altering calorie absorption or energy expenditure.
source: Thus, while it is possible that the inaccuracies inherent to food intake measurement prevented us from detecting an alteration in food intake in the CckTetTox animals, silencing NTSCck neurons might impact body weight by other means, including by altering calorie absorption or energy expenditure.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the body weight phenotype.

claim: NTSCck neurons contribute to the long-term control of energy balance.
source: In any case, NTSCck neurons, like NTSCalcr and NTSLepr cells, contribute to the long-term control of energy balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased body weight observed in CckTetTox mice on HFD.

claim: HFD-fed CckTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of VSG surgery.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed CckTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG promoted similar weight loss in these animals as in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VSG promoted similar weight loss in CckTetTox mice as in controls.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed CckTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG promoted similar weight loss in these animals as in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: CNO treatment promoted FOS-IR in the NTS of LCKDq mice.
source: As expected, CNO treatment promoted FOS-IR in the NTS of LCKDq mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed and HFD-fed LCKDq mice.
source: As for LCDq mice (Figure 1), CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed and HFD-fed LCKDq mice, and strongly suppressed refeeding following an overnight fast (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: CNO strongly suppressed refeeding following an overnight fast in LCKDq mice.
source: As for LCDq mice (Figure 1), CNO almost completely abrogated food intake at the onset of the dark cycle in chow-fed and HFD-fed LCKDq mice, and strongly suppressed refeeding following an overnight fast (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CNO treatment dramatically decreased food intake in LCKDq mice over a two-day treatment.
source: We also assessed the effect of activating NTSLCK neurons over a two-day treatment. CNO treatment dramatically decreased food intake in LCKDq mice and resulted in even larger decreases in body weight that in LCDq mice (Figures 1E–F–4E–F), confirming the effectiveness of the coordinated action of NTSLCK neurons for the control of food intake and body weight.
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic treatment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CNO treatment resulted in even larger decreases in body weight in LCKDq mice than in LCDq mice.
source: We also assessed the effect of activating NTSLCK neurons over a two-day treatment. CNO treatment dramatically decreased food intake in LCKDq mice and resulted in even larger decreases in body weight that in LCDq mice (Figures 1E–F–4E–F), confirming the effectiveness of the coordinated action of NTSLCK neurons for the control of food intake and body weight.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of body weight data in Figures 1F and 4F.

claim: The coordinated action of NTSLCK neurons is effective for the control of food intake and body weight.
source: We also assessed the effect of activating NTSLCK neurons over a two-day treatment. CNO treatment dramatically decreased food intake in LCKDq mice and resulted in even larger decreases in body weight that in LCDq mice (Figures 1E–F–4E–F), confirming the effectiveness of the coordinated action of NTSLCK neurons for the control of food intake and body weight.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dramatic effects on food intake and body weight.

claim: The activation of NTSCck neurons may promote negative energy balance by altering energy absorption or expenditure as well as by decreasing feeding.
source: Because food intake during CNO treatment was similarly low for LCDq and LCKDq mice (it is not possible to decrease food intake below zero), while the LCKDq mice lost more body weight, it is possible that the activation of NTSCck neurons promotes negative energy balance by altering energy absorption or expenditure as well as by decreasing feeding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of greater weight loss in LCKDq mice despite similar food intake suppression.

claim: Silencing NTSCck cells increased body weight without measurably altering food intake.
source: Indeed, silencing NTSCck cells increased body weight without measurably altering food intake (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to HFD.
source: We also found that, unlike NTSLC cells, activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to HFD or saccharine in water, consistent with the avoidance-provoking nature of NTSCck neurons and the dominant nature of avoidance-provoking over non-avoidance-provoking hindbrain signals (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to saccharine in water.
source: We also found that, unlike NTSLC cells, activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to HFD or saccharine in water, consistent with the avoidance-provoking nature of NTSCck neurons and the dominant nature of avoidance-provoking over non-avoidance-provoking hindbrain signals (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CTA assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The CTA provoked by activating NTSLCK cells is consistent with the avoidance-provoking nature of NTSCck neurons.
source: We also found that, unlike NTSLC cells, activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to HFD or saccharine in water, consistent with the avoidance-provoking nature of NTSCck neurons and the dominant nature of avoidance-provoking over non-avoidance-provoking hindbrain signals (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CTA data in the context of prior knowledge about NTSCck neurons.

claim: The CTA provoked by activating NTSLCK cells is consistent with the dominant nature of avoidance-provoking over non-avoidance-provoking hindbrain signals.
source: We also found that, unlike NTSLC cells, activating NTSLCK cells provoked a strong CTA to HFD or saccharine in water, consistent with the avoidance-provoking nature of NTSCck neurons and the dominant nature of avoidance-provoking over non-avoidance-provoking hindbrain signals (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CTA data suggesting dominance of aversive signals.

claim: LCKTetTox mice displayed a significant increase in food intake on chow.
source: While we had not detected increased food intake on chow diet in LeprTetTox, CalcrTetTox, CckTetTox, or LCTetTox animals (Figures 2–3), LCKTetTox mice displayed a significant increase in food intake on chow, as well as on HFD (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: LCKTetTox mice displayed a significant increase in food intake on HFD.
source: While we had not detected increased food intake on chow diet in LeprTetTox, CalcrTetTox, CckTetTox, or LCTetTox animals (Figures 2–3), LCKTetTox mice displayed a significant increase in food intake on chow, as well as on HFD (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LCKTetTox mice tended to gain more weight on chow diet, but the effect was not statistically significant.
source: Although LCKTetTox mice also tended to gain more weight on chow diet, the effect was not statistically significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LCKTetTox mice became significantly heavier than controls after the first week on HFD.
source: However, these animals became significantly heavier than controls after the first week on HFD, and continued to gain weight relative to controls with each additional week (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LCKTetTox mice continued to gain weight relative to controls with each additional week on HFD.
source: However, these animals became significantly heavier than controls after the first week on HFD, and continued to gain weight relative to controls with each additional week (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LCKTetTox animals displayed increased HFD food intake compared to CckTetTox and LCTetTox mice.
source: While one must exercise caution when comparing results among different strains of mice, we observed increased HFD food intake for LCKTetTox animals compared to CckTetTox and LCTetTox mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative food intake data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: LCKTetTox mice tended to gain more weight on HFD compared to LCTetTox and CckTetTox animals.
source: Similarly, LCKTetTox mice tended to gain more weight on HFD compared to LCTetTox and CckTetTox animals (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative body weight data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Simultaneously silencing multiple food intake controlling NTS neuron populations cumulatively increases food intake and body weight, irrespective of whether or not the neurons mediate avoidance responses.
source: These findings suggest that simultaneously silencing multiple food intake controlling NTS neuron populations cumulatively increases food intake and body weight, irrespective of whether or not the neurons mediate avoidance responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of effects across different TetTox mouse lines.

claim: CNO provoked little AP FOS-IR in LeprDq mice.
source: While CNO provoked little AP FOS-IR in LeprDq mice, the activation of NTSCalcr or NTSCck neurons tended to increase AP FOS-IR (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The activation of NTSCalcr or NTSCck neurons tended to increase AP FOS-IR.
source: While CNO provoked little AP FOS-IR in LeprDq mice, the activation of NTSCalcr or NTSCck neurons tended to increase AP FOS-IR (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CNO treatment in LCDq mice did not increase AP FOS-IR compared to that observed in CalcrDq mice.
source: Furthermore, while CNO treatment in LCDq mice did not increase AP FOS-IR compared to that observed in CalcrDq mice, LCKDq demonstrated the greatest amount of AP FOS-IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LCKDq mice demonstrated the greatest amount of AP FOS-IR.
source: Furthermore, while CNO treatment in LCDq mice did not increase AP FOS-IR compared to that observed in CalcrDq mice, LCKDq demonstrated the greatest amount of AP FOS-IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LCDq mice demonstrated increased PBN FOS-IR compared to LeprDq or CalcrDq alone.
source: In the PBN (Figure 6B and D), the LCDq mice demonstrated increased FOS-IR compared to LeprDq or CalcrDq alone, although neither of these induced the colocalization of FOS-IR with CGRP (the activation of which is known to promote avoidance behavior Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neither LeprDq nor CalcrDq mice induced the colocalization of FOS-IR with CGRP in the PBN.
source: In the PBN (Figure 6B and D), the LCDq mice demonstrated increased FOS-IR compared to LeprDq or CalcrDq alone, although neither of these induced the colocalization of FOS-IR with CGRP (the activation of which is known to promote avoidance behavior Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS/CGRP colocalization data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The activation of CGRP neurons is known to promote avoidance behavior.
source: In the PBN (Figure 6B and D), the LCDq mice demonstrated increased FOS-IR compared to LeprDq or CalcrDq alone, although neither of these induced the colocalization of FOS-IR with CGRP (the activation of which is known to promote avoidance behavior Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The activation of NTSCck cells alone or in combination with the other cell types provoked FOS/CGRP colocalization in the PBN.
source: In contrast, the activation of NTSCck cells alone or in combination with the other cell types provoked FOS/CGRP colocalization, consistent with the avoidance response provoked by any stimulus that includes the activation of NTSCck cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS/CGRP colocalization data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: FOS/CGRP colocalization in the PBN is consistent with the avoidance response provoked by any stimulus that includes the activation of NTSCck cells.
source: In contrast, the activation of NTSCck cells alone or in combination with the other cell types provoked FOS/CGRP colocalization, consistent with the avoidance response provoked by any stimulus that includes the activation of NTSCck cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FOS/CGRP colocalization data.

claim: CNO treatment in LCKDq mice provoked increased PBN FOS-IR compared to LCDq mice.
source: CNO treatment in LCKDq mice provoked increased PBN FOS-IR compared to LCDq mice, suggesting the existence of substantial numbers of distinct PBN targets for NTSCck compared to NTSLC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR quantification shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There exist substantial numbers of distinct PBN targets for NTSCck compared to NTSLC neurons.
source: CNO treatment in LCKDq mice provoked increased PBN FOS-IR compared to LCDq mice, suggesting the existence of substantial numbers of distinct PBN targets for NTSCck compared to NTSLC neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased PBN FOS-IR in LCKDq compared to LCDq mice.

claim: The activation of DMH FOS-IR increased with the stimulation of additional NTS cell types.
source: The activation of DMH FOS-IR similarly increased with the stimulation of additional NTS cell types (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each NTS population targets at least partially distinct downstream neurons in several brain regions.
source: Together, these findings suggest that each NTS population targets at least partially distinct downstream neurons in several brain regions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential patterns of FOS-IR in downstream regions.

claim: The activation of additional downstream targets by the stimulation of more populations of NTS neurons likely underlies the cumulative effects of activating multiple NTS cell types.
source: Thus, the activation of additional downstream targets by the stimulation of more populations of NTS neurons likely underlies the cumulative effects of activating multiple NTS cell types.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying cumulative effects.

claim: HFD-fed LCKTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of VSG surgery.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed LCKTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG promoted more body and fat mass loss in these animals than in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: VSG promoted more body and fat mass loss in LCKTetTox mice than in controls.
source: While, as expected, HFD-fed LCKTetTox mice weighed more than HFD-fed control animals at the time of surgery, VSG promoted more body and fat mass loss in these animals than in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Food intake was decreased by VSG in LCKTetTox animals.
source: Food intake was decreased by VSG in LCKTetTox animals, although it remained higher than for control mice that had received VSG, presumably reflecting the increased food intake of these mice at baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Food intake in LCKTetTox mice after VSG remained higher than for control mice that had received VSG.
source: Food intake was decreased by VSG in LCKTetTox animals, although it remained higher than for control mice that had received VSG, presumably reflecting the increased food intake of these mice at baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The higher food intake in LCKTetTox mice after VSG presumably reflects the increased food intake of these mice at baseline.
source: Food intake was decreased by VSG in LCKTetTox animals, although it remained higher than for control mice that had received VSG, presumably reflecting the increased food intake of these mice at baseline.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the food intake data.

claim: VSG normalized body weight and fat mass in LCKTetTox mice.
source: Thus, VSG normalized body weight and fat mass in LCKTetTox mice and promoted similar improvements in indices of glucose homeostasis in LCKTetTox and control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by VSG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: VSG promoted similar improvements in indices of glucose homeostasis in LCKTetTox and control mice.
source: Thus, VSG normalized body weight and fat mass in LCKTetTox mice and promoted similar improvements in indices of glucose homeostasis in LCKTetTox and control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2J-L.

claim: Neurons other than NTSLCK cells must mediate the response to VSG.
source: These findings suggest that, despite the important roles for these cells in the physiologic restraint of feeding and body weight, neurons other than NTSLCK cells must mediate the response to VSG.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VSG is still effective when NTSLCK cells are silenced.

claim: NTSLCK cells represent approximately 20% of feeding-activated NTS neurons in control mice.
source: This analysis revealed that NTSLCK cells represent approximately 20% of feeding-activated NTS neurons in control mice, and approximately 35% of such neurons following VSG.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR colocalization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: NTSLCK cells represent approximately 35% of feeding-activated NTS neurons following VSG.
source: This analysis revealed that NTSLCK cells represent approximately 20% of feeding-activated NTS neurons in control mice, and approximately 35% of such neurons following VSG.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR colocalization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Feeding stimulates non-LCK neurons in the NTS.
source: Thus, in addition to neurons in the AP, hypothalamus, and elsewhere, feeding stimulates non-LCK neurons in the NTS and these feeding-activated non-LCK cells presumably contribute to food intake suppression and body weight control.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that many FOS+ neurons are not LCK neurons.

claim: Feeding-activated non-LCK cells presumably contribute to food intake suppression and body weight control.
source: Thus, in addition to neurons in the AP, hypothalamus, and elsewhere, feeding stimulates non-LCK neurons in the NTS and these feeding-activated non-LCK cells presumably contribute to food intake suppression and body weight control.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that these cells are activated by feeding.

claim: Distinct groups of food intake-inhibiting NTS neurons act cumulatively to suppress food intake under physiologic feeding as well as during artificial activation.
source: Our findings reveal that distinct groups of food intake-inhibiting NTS neurons act cumulatively to suppress food intake under physiologic feeding as well as during artificial activation.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The enhanced suppression of food intake mediated by the activation of multiple populations of individually non-aversive NTS neurons does not promote avoidance responses irrespective of the strength of food intake suppression.
source: We also show that the enhanced suppression of food intake mediated by the activation of multiple populations of individually non-aversive NTS neurons does not promote avoidance responses irrespective of the strength of food intake suppression, consistent with the notion that the pathways that promote the non-aversive suppression of food intake are distinct from those that promote avoidance responses.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the CTA data.

claim: The pathways that promote the non-aversive suppression of food intake are distinct from those that promote avoidance responses.
source: We also show that the enhanced suppression of food intake mediated by the activation of multiple populations of individually non-aversive NTS neurons does not promote avoidance responses irrespective of the strength of food intake suppression, consistent with the notion that the pathways that promote the non-aversive suppression of food intake are distinct from those that promote avoidance responses.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that non-aversive neurons don't cause CTA even when strongly suppressing feeding.

claim: NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons individually and coordinately restrain body weight gain during HFD feeding.
source: Finally, although NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons individually and coordinately restrain body weight gain during HFD feeding but these cells are dispensable for weight loss in response to VSG and feeding activates additional NTS cell types, suggesting roles for additional neuron types (including within the NTS) in feeding suppression.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the TetTox experiments.

claim: NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons are dispensable for weight loss in response to VSG.
source: Finally, although NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons individually and coordinately restrain body weight gain during HFD feeding but these cells are dispensable for weight loss in response to VSG and feeding activates additional NTS cell types, suggesting roles for additional neuron types (including within the NTS) in feeding suppression.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the VSG experiments in TetTox mice.

claim: Feeding activates additional NTS cell types beyond NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons.
source: Finally, although NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons individually and coordinately restrain body weight gain during HFD feeding but these cells are dispensable for weight loss in response to VSG and feeding activates additional NTS cell types, suggesting roles for additional neuron types (including within the NTS) in feeding suppression.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the FOS-IR data.

claim: Additional neuron types (including within the NTS) play roles in feeding suppression.
source: Finally, although NTSLepr, NTSCalcr, and NTSCck neurons individually and coordinately restrain body weight gain during HFD feeding but these cells are dispensable for weight loss in response to VSG and feeding activates additional NTS cell types, suggesting roles for additional neuron types (including within the NTS) in feeding suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the VSG and FOS-IR data.

claim: Calcr and Lepr expression do not colocalize in the same NTS neurons.
source: Calcr and Lepr expression do not colocalize in the same NTS neurons and unbiased clustering methods reveal that NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons map to distinct populations of NTS neurons in mice (NTSCalcr neurons map to GLU11, while NTSLepr neurons map mainly to GLU13 and GLU2; GLU13 controls feeding) (Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSCalcr neurons map to GLU11.
source: Calcr and Lepr expression do not colocalize in the same NTS neurons and unbiased clustering methods reveal that NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons map to distinct populations of NTS neurons in mice (NTSCalcr neurons map to GLU11, while NTSLepr neurons map mainly to GLU13 and GLU2; GLU13 controls feeding) (Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSLepr neurons map mainly to GLU13 and GLU2.
source: Calcr and Lepr expression do not colocalize in the same NTS neurons and unbiased clustering methods reveal that NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons map to distinct populations of NTS neurons in mice (NTSCalcr neurons map to GLU11, while NTSLepr neurons map mainly to GLU13 and GLU2; GLU13 controls feeding) (Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GLU13 controls feeding.
source: Calcr and Lepr expression do not colocalize in the same NTS neurons and unbiased clustering methods reveal that NTSCalcr and NTSLepr neurons map to distinct populations of NTS neurons in mice (NTSCalcr neurons map to GLU11, while NTSLepr neurons map mainly to GLU13 and GLU2; GLU13 controls feeding) (Ludwig et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Each of NTSCalcr and NTSLepr populations strongly suppresses food intake but fails to promote a CTA when activated.
source: Each of these populations strongly suppresses food intake but fails to promote a CTA when activated, suggesting that these NTS cells activate pathways that blunt feeding without engaging distinct avoidance pathways (Cheng et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017; Tsang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSCalcr and NTSLepr cells activate pathways that blunt feeding without engaging distinct avoidance pathways.
source: Each of these populations strongly suppresses food intake but fails to promote a CTA when activated, suggesting that these NTS cells activate pathways that blunt feeding without engaging distinct avoidance pathways (Cheng et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2020a; Cheng et al., 2020b; Gaykema et al., 2017; Tsang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that these cells suppress feeding without causing CTA.

claim: The finding that the combined activation of NTSCalcr and NTSLepr cells reduces feeding by >90% over the first 24 hr of treatment, but fails to promote a CTA, reinforces the notion that brainstem pathways need not provoke aversive responses to suppress food intake.
source: Our finding that the combined activation of these two cell types reduces feeding by >90% over the first 24 hr of treatment, but fails to promote a CTA, further reinforces the notion that brainstem pathways need not provoke aversive responses to suppress food intake.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The magnitude of the anorexia that accompanies the combined activation of NTSCalcr and NTSLepr cells relative to the response to the activation of a single population reveals that distinct populations of food intake-suppressing NTS neurons can act cumulatively to suppress feeding more effectively.
source: The magnitude of the anorexia that accompanies the combined activation of NTSCalcr and NTSLepr cells relative to the response to the activation of a single population also reveals that distinct populations of food intake-suppressing NTS neurons can act cumulatively to suppress feeding more effectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The effects of the various sets of food intake-suppressing NTS neurons must augment each other to suppress physiologic feeding, at least under HFD-fed conditions.
source: Hence, the effects of the various sets of food intake-suppressing NTS neurons must augment each other to suppress physiologic feeding, at least under HFD-fed conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the cumulative effects observed in TetTox experiments.

claim: The distribution of evoked FOS-IR varies somewhat between NTS cell types.
source: Indeed, the distribution of evoked FOS-IR varies somewhat between NTS cell types; unlike NTSCalcr and NTSCck cells, NTSLepr neurons poorly activate AP cells, while NTSCck cells (but not NTSCalcr and/or NTSLepr cells) activate PBN CGRP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the FOS-IR distribution data.

claim: Unlike NTSCalcr and NTSCck cells, NTSLepr neurons poorly activate AP cells.
source: Indeed, the distribution of evoked FOS-IR varies somewhat between NTS cell types; unlike NTSCalcr and NTSCck cells, NTSLepr neurons poorly activate AP cells, while NTSCck cells (but not NTSCalcr and/or NTSLepr cells) activate PBN CGRP neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS-IR data in Figure 6.

claim: NTSCck cells (but not NTSCalcr and/or NTSLepr cells) activate PBN CGRP neurons.
source: Indeed, the distribution of evoked FOS-IR varies somewhat between NTS cell types; unlike NTSCalcr and NTSCck cells, NTSLepr neurons poorly activate AP cells, while NTSCck cells (but not NTSCalcr and/or NTSLepr cells) activate PBN CGRP neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by FOS/CGRP colocalization data in Figure 6B.

claim: The finding that silencing NTSCalcr, NTSLepr, and NTSCck cells increases food intake and body weight in HFD-fed animals, but barely (if at all) alters these parameters in chow-fed animals indicates the importance of these cells for the restraint of food intake specifically during the consumption of palatable calorically dense food.
source: The finding that silencing NTSCalcr, NTSLepr, and NTSCck cells increases food intake and body weight in HFD-fed animals, but barely (if at all) alters these parameters in chow-fed animals indicates the importance of these cells for the restraint of food intake specifically during the consumption of palatable calorically dense food.
